opus-5.5.text:
I think the change is quite fundamental. In Kaiming's era, roughly 2015 to 2020, a single researcher or a small group with a few GPUs could come up with an idea like ResNet, test it on ImageNet, and change the whole field. The bottleneck was the idea itself. If you had good intuition about architectures, normalization, or training tricks, you could validate it in a few weeks and the community would adopt it quickly. That was a golden period for algorithm research in academia.

Now, with large language models, a lot has shifted. Many of the most important questions only show up at scale. A trick that helps a small model may disappear or even hurt at a hundred billion parameters. So the cost of verifying an idea has gone up enormously, and much of the frontier work has moved into companies with large clusters. For a student or a small lab, competing head-on on pretraining algorithms is very hard.

But I don't think the opportunities have disappeared. They've moved. First, the systems side has become much more important. When models are this big, how you serve them, schedule them, and use memory efficiently directly decides whether an algorithm is practical. That's part of why I've spent so much time on inference infrastructure. Infrastructure is now part of algorithm research. Second, there's a lot of room in post-training, reasoning, evaluation, and understanding why these models behave the way they do. Those areas still reward cleverness more than raw compute. Third, open-source has become a new kind of research platform. If you build something many people use, you get feedback and impact that a single paper often can't.

So I'd say the era of "one elegant idea on one benchmark" is mostly behind us. The era now rewards people who understand the whole stack, from the math to the hardware, and who can find the problems that big labs are too busy or too structured to look at carefully. It's harder in some ways, but in others there's more to do than ever.

r001.rationale: The response says a small group with a few GPUs could make influential advances, but does not attribute the era’s greater opportunities to fewer researchers entering the field.

r002.rationale: It says one-idea advances are mostly behind us and that frontier research now requires scale, but does not connect exhausted low-hanging fruit to the difficulty of fundamental advances.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention scaling laws or the belief that more compute and data can improve performance without changing the basic algorithm.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest change is that the "cheap" opportunities are mostly gone. When Kaiming did ResNet, the field was still in a stage where one person with a few GPUs and a good idea could change everything. The problem space was wide open, the baselines were weak, and a clean insight like residual connections could give you a huge jump. That kind of research was high-leverage and low-cost. A PhD student in a university lab could do it.

Today the situation is very different. The frontier has moved to large models, and the cost of validating an idea at scale is enormous. If you want to prove something really matters, you often need thousands of GPUs and a team of engineers, not a single student and a clever trick. Many ideas that look great at small scale simply disappear when you scale up, so the bar for "this is a real contribution" is much higher. Academia, honestly, is somewhat squeezed out of the core algorithm game. The big results now mostly come from industry labs.

But I don't think opportunities have gone away, they've just shifted. A few places I see them.

First, systems and infrastructure. Working on vLLM made me realize that how you run a model is now as important as what the model is. Inference efficiency, scheduling, memory management, distributed execution: these problems are concrete, open source, and you can make an impact without owning a giant cluster. A lot of the "algorithm" value today actually lives at the boundary between algorithm and system.

Second, the open-source ecosystem itself. In Kaiming's era, influence came from papers. Now it increasingly comes from code that people actually use. If your work ends up in the stack that everyone deploys, that's a kind of impact that didn't exist in the same way before.

Third, there are still real scientific questions, they just look different. Understanding why scaling works, data quality, post-training, reasoning, long context. Many of these are not solved, and some can be studied with modest compute if you are smart about experimental design.

So my view is: the era of "one brilliant idea from a small lab reshapes the field" is largely over, at least for now. But the era of "a careful engineer-researcher who understands the whole stack can have outsized impact" is just beginning. The skill set required is broader. You need to understand algorithms, but also hardware, systems, and how things actually get used. That's less romantic than the ResNet story, but in some ways it's more honest about where the real leverage is today.

r001.rationale: The response says the field was more open and a small lab could make an impact, but it does not attribute that opportunity to fewer researchers having entered the field.

r002.rationale: It says cheap opportunities and the era of a single idea reshaping the field are largely over, and describes the higher bar for making a real contribution today.

r003.rationale: It mentions scaling and lists understanding why scaling works as an open question, but does not define a belief that more compute and data improve performance without changing the basic algorithm.

astra-6.text:
I think the opportunities are still there, but the conditions have changed. In Professor Kaiming He’s era, it was more feasible for a small research group to propose an architectural idea, test it on a widely used benchmark, and have that idea influence the whole field. Today, especially with large models, testing an idea at a convincing scale can require substantial compute and engineering resources.

That makes some kinds of algorithm research harder for individual researchers, but it also creates new questions. How can we train with less compute? How can we make inference cheaper? How can we use data more effectively? Those constraints are themselves opportunities for algorithmic innovation.

So I wouldn’t say that the era of algorithm research is over. I’d say that choosing the right problem matters more. A useful approach is to get close to real systems, understand where they struggle, and find a problem where a clear insight can make a measurable difference. You don’t necessarily need to compete on the scale of the largest training run to do meaningful work.

r002.rationale: It discusses the resource demands of large-scale research, but does not say low-hanging fruit has been exhausted or that this makes fundamental advances harder.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the opportunities are still there, but the conditions have changed. In Professor Kaiming He’s era, a relatively small team could explore an architectural idea and demonstrate a very substantial improvement. Today, if you want to improve a frontier model directly, the compute, data, and engineering requirements can make that much harder for an individual researcher.

But I wouldn’t conclude that algorithm research has fewer opportunities overall. The questions have shifted. How do we make models more efficient? How do we get more learning out of limited data or compute? And how do we identify limitations that scaling alone doesn’t resolve? Those are all algorithmic questions.

For a young researcher, I think the key is to find a question where you can run convincing experiments with the resources you have. You don’t necessarily need to compete on the largest training run. You need a clear insight and a way to test it.

r001.rationale: It says a relatively small team could demonstrate large improvements, but does not attribute that opportunity to fewer researchers having entered the field.

r002.rationale: It says direct frontier-model improvements are harder today, but does not connect that difficulty to low-hanging algorithmic advances being exhausted.

r003.rationale: It mentions compute, data, and scaling, but does not identify the belief that increasing them can improve performance without changing the basic algorithm.
